speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The Ministry of Finance and Customs regularly review the Customs Act to ensure that the Act remains up to date and in line with policy intent.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The Customs Act was last amended in 2012.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: A public consultation exercise on the draft Bill was held from 9 May to 5 June last year.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The Ministry of Finance (MOF) and Customs have published a summary of comments received and our responses.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The first set of amendments seeks to support policy changes on fuel taxes.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: At the same time, the existing lump sum special tax on diesel vehicles was reduced.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The shift from a lump sum tax to a usage-based tax was to incentivise users to reduce diesel consumption.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We have three amendments in the Bill to support these tax changes.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: First, we will broaden the definition of “motor fuel” in the Customs Act to include diesel and any fuel that may be used to power a means of transport.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The Customs Act empowers Customs to enforce revenue collection and customs laws relating to motor fuels that attract duties.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: For instance, by law, Singapore-registered vehicles are required to have a minimum amount of motor fuel – three quarters of the tank – when leaving Singapore at land checkpoints.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This is to prevent drivers from evading payment of Singapore’s fuel duties.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: However, the current definition of "motor fuel", which these laws rely on, only includes petrol and compressed natural gas (CNG), but not diesel.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: With the introduction of volume-based duty on diesel, there is a need to include diesel in the definition, so that Customs can enforce the relevant rules.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, we have broadened the definition of “motor fuel” to include any fuel, including diesel, that can power a means of transport.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Second, we will amend the Act to clarify the processes by which Customs will deal with changes to the rate of special taxes for motor vehicles.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Currently, special tax is levied on diesel vehicles and is paid together with the tax for the vehicle licence for either a six-month or a 12-month period.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The Customs Act does not state what happens when the special tax rate is changed in the middle of a period that has already been paid for, or the "current period" for short.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: For instance, the special tax rate was reduced at Budget 2017, on 20 February 2017, which would have been during the current period for some vehicle owners.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, we need to amend the Act to provide greater clarity going forward on how the amount of special tax payable should be calculated when there are different special tax rates within the current period.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In particular, the amendment will allow the Minister for Finance to prescribe the effective date of the new rate and the treatment for overpayment or underpayment of special tax.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: For example, the Minister can prescribe that any overpayment can be offset against any other tax, levy or fee payable under the Road Traffic Act in respect of the motor vehicle.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Clauses 7 to 9 provide for these changes.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Third, we will give authorised Customs officers the discretion to let vehicles which have flouted the three-quarter tank rule, but cannot U-turn at the checkpoint, to leave Singapore after imposing the fine.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: I spoke earlier about the minimum motor fuel requirement for motorists departing Singapore.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Currently, motorists caught flouting this rule at the land checkpoints will be fined and must U-turn to top up their fuel tank before they can leave Singapore.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: With the expanded definition of "motor fuel" mentioned earlier, the rule will now apply to diesel-powered vehicles.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But it may not always be possible for larger diesel-powered vehicles like coaches and trucks, to U-turn if they are caught, due to infrastructure constraints.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, for practical reasons, such motorists have to be allowed to leave Singapore while still being held liable for trying to leave Singapore without the required minimum amount of fuel.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Clause 15 gives Customs officers the discretion to allow this.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Customs will explore imposing a comparatively higher penalty for such vehicles, to maintain parity with vehicles made to U-turn.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Next, I move to the second set of amendments which seeks to improve Customs' efficiency in carrying out its daily operations, and there are three key changes.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Short-levied and erroneously refunded duties can arise due to incorrect calculations or deliberate attempts to defraud Customs on the duties and GST payable.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Some cases of underpaid duties and GST may only be uncovered more than one year after the event of underpayment.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, this change will give Customs greater operational flexibility to seek the recovery of short-levied and erroneously refunded duties and GST.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The revised time limit will be aligned with the requirement for companies to keep records for five years under the Income Tax Act and GST Act, and clause 11 provides for the changes.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Such situations can arise when traders, after tallying their accounts at the end of their financial year or through audits, realise that they have overpaid duties and GST on their import permit applications made more than a year ago.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, this amendment will give more time for traders to discover any errors in payment to Customs.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And this will also align the time allowance in the Customs Act with that of the GST Act.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Currently, approval from the Minister for Finance is required for DG-Customs to delegate any of his powers to senior officers of Customs.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Some powers, such as waiver of payment and granting of licences, may need to be delegated from time to time to ensure efficiency of Customs’ daily operations.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: These powers tend to be operational in nature.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And this amendment will streamline the administrative processes for such delegation.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This particular amendment also aligns the administration of the Customs Act with that of the GST Act and the Regulation of Imports and Exports Act (RIEA).

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: These latter two Acts empower the Comptroller and DG-Customs to delegate powers without needing to seek the approval of the Minister for Finance or the Minister for Trade and Industry respectively.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Next, I turn to the amendments to provide legal clarity to current policies and I would like to highlight two key changes pertaining to collection and reimposition of duties.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Duties and import GST are imposed on goods imported into Singapore for use and consumption.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: On the other hand, transshipment goods stored in the FTZs, which are designated areas at the ports and airport that facilitate entrepot trade, enjoy temporary suspension of customs or excise duties and import GST, as they are not meant for usage and consumption here.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: However, if these goods are used or consumed within the FTZs, then the suspension ceases to apply.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Currently, the Act is worded generally to impose liability for duties and GST for any goods in FTZs that cannot be accounted for.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This change will provide legal clarity that goods used or consumed within FTZs are liable for duties and GST, in line with the existing policy intent.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Certain goods may enjoy duty exemption upon import, and then be liable for duties later on when the conditions of the exemption no longer hold.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: One example is that embassies are entitled to duty exemption when they import motor vehicles for official use.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But if the motor vehicle is subsequently sold to a person that is not eligible for the exemption, the duty exemption will cease to apply, and duties will need to be levied and paid on the motor vehicle.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Customs currently reimposes duties on a good based on its value either at importation, or when the exemption expires, depending on the circumstances.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This is determined by Customs based on factors, such as the nature of the good and the conditions of the exemption.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, this amendment will provide clarity in the Act that Customs has the flexibility to reimpose duties based on the value either at importation, or when the exemption ceases.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In summary, Mr Speaker, the Bill will help Customs to implement the recent tax changes on diesel and enable Customs to carry out its day-to-day operations more efficiently.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The Bill will also provide legal clarity to current policies.
